title: America Almost Ate Hippo Meat — Illustrated Story Pilot
negative_prompt: generic documentary b-roll, static slideshow composition, empty landscapes, unreadable text, malformed lettering, duplicated animals, extra limbs, gore, attack close-up, plastic CGI skin, modern objects in 1910 scenes, fake government seals, fake network logos, oversaturated teal-orange grading, centered subject in every frame

worlds.base_prompt: Premium editorial illustrated-history frame with dimensional lighting, tactile period detail, playful visual exaggeration, crisp readable props, strong foreground-middle-background composition, cinematic 16:9 framing. Every frame must communicate a story beat while muted. Period scenes are historically grounded 1910 America; alternate-history scenes are visually absurd but photorealistically coherent. Use visual comedy through juxtaposition, scale and reactions rather than cartoon styling.

narration.narration: This burger almost wasn't beef. In another America, the family cookout, the grocery aisle, even the diner special could have meant one enormous thing: hippo.
The strange part is this wasn't a joke. In 1910, meat prices were a political problem, and Americans were hunting for a new source of cheap protein.
One proposal sounded impossible: bring hippopotamuses to Louisiana, let them eat invasive water plants, then turn the animals themselves into dinner.
Now picture the plan actually working. Bayous become hippo ranches. Butchers learn a whole new animal. Menus stop looking strange because hippo becomes normal.
It never became the American dinner table. But that ordinary burger is now a reminder: history isn't only what happened. It's also the weird futures we barely avoided.
